Iran struck what it called hostile targets in the Strait of Hormuz after explosions near Qeshm Island, and the Iran-Oman draft now in front of the Iranian parliament is far more restrictive than markets had priced: US and Israeli vessels barred, compensation demanded from countries Tehran deems hostile, penalties of 20% of cargo value for violations, and NO full reopening until the US naval blockade is lifted. The Fed repricing flipped with it: Lisa Cook said in Anchorage that inflation is too high and she is prepared to raise rates, Warsh is open to September if inflation reaccelerates, and the September hike is BACK in the price. meta.regime: The de-escalation regime that drove the last three sessions has broken, and every leg of yesterday's board has to be re-cut. Iran struck what it described as hostile targets in the Strait of Hormuz following explosions near Qeshm Island, and the terms of the Iran-Oman draft now under review by the Iranian parliament turned out to be materially harsher than the market had assumed: Tehran wants US and Israeli vessels barred from transit, wants countries it deems hostile to pay compensation before passage, has proposed penalties equal to 20% of a vessel's cargo value for violations, and has stated that a full reopening depends on the US lifting its maritime blockade. Iranian officials said explicitly that the Oman arrangement will not fully reopen the strait. This is the opposite of what was priced. WTI has recovered to $77.72 from $74.79, a two-session move of roughly 4% that leaves it up 5.7% on the month and 21.7% on the year, with Brent at $83.28. The second-order effect is the important one: higher crude re-arms the inflation path, which re-arms the Fed. Governor Lisa Cook told an Anchorage audience that inflation is too high and that she considers the inflation risk greater than the employment risk, saying she is prepared to act by raising rates; Chair Warsh has said he is open to September if inflation reaccelerates. The soft-labour narrative that drove yesterday's dollar break has also thinned out - initial claims were 199k with the four-week average at 198,750, the lowest of this cycle, announced layoffs were the lowest in two years, productivity rose 1.4% and unit labour costs came in at 1.3%, roughly half the expected pace, which is outright disinflationary. ADP at 44k and the ISM services employment index at 47.4 still stand, but they no longer stand alone. The dollar is therefore upgraded from -1 back to 0 into a payroll print that lands at 12:30Z today. The metals have split: silver has fallen for two straight sessions to $62.03 because higher oil means higher inflation means a live September hike, while gold holds $4,250.77 on the returning haven bid. The euro keeps the top of the board and arguably strengthens - the ECB's own July commentary tied its hiking case to energy, so a crude rebound raises rather than lowers the odds of the September 10 move.
meta.nextBigEvent: US July employment report, today Aug 7 12:30Z (consensus around +91k after +57k; unemployment seen 4.3% from 4.2%)

dailyRead: Yesterday's board was built on a Hormuz reopening and it has to come off. Iran struck what it called hostile targets in the strait after explosions near Qeshm Island, and the draft agreement the Iranian parliament is now reviewing is far more restrictive than anything the market had in the price: US and Israeli vessels barred from transit, compensation payable by countries Tehran considers hostile, penalties equal to 20% of a vessel's cargo value for violations, and no full reopening at all until the US lifts its naval blockade. Iranian officials have said outright that the Oman corridor does not reopen the waterway. Yesterday's file described a 60-day interim deal with no transit fees; that framing was wrong and is corrected here. WTI is back at $77.72 from $74.79, up 5.7% over the month with Brent at $83.28, and the whole rates complex has followed it. Lisa Cook used a speech in Anchorage to say that inflation is too high, that she rates the inflation risk above the employment risk, and that she is prepared to raise rates; Warsh has said September is open if inflation reaccelerates. Against that, the labour case for a dovish Fed has quietly weakened - initial claims printed 199k with a four-week average of 198,750 that is the lowest of the cycle, announced layoffs were the lowest in two years, and unit labour costs rose just 1.3%, around half the expected pace. ADP at 44k and ISM services employment at 47.4 have not been erased, but they are no longer the only reads on the table, and the September hike is back in the price. USD therefore goes from -1 to 0, which collapses most of yesterday's dollar-leg trades: EUR/USD drops from HIGH to MEDIUM, GBP/USD and AUD/USD to LOW-MED, USD/JPY and USD/CAD to RANGE, and USD/CHF actually flips to a small LONG. The yen is the other downgrade. The wage story is intact and the Bank of Japan has warned that underlying inflation could exceed target, but the currency has given back its intervention gains with USD/JPY at 158.40 against a 155.20 spike, the 10-year JGB is at 2.79% and rising on the oil move, and higher crude is the single worst input for the G10's largest energy importer. JPY goes from +1 to 0 and the yen-cross shorts come off with it - NZD/JPY drops to MEDIUM, CAD/JPY and USD/JPY to RANGE. Canada is the mirror image: WTI at $78 restores the terms-of-trade leg, so CAD is upgraded from -1 to 0, and note the correction that June employment was +18k with unemployment at 6.5% and wages at 3.3%, not the +87.8k in yesterday's file. The euro stays at +2 and the case is stronger, not weaker, because the ECB explicitly hung its hiking bias on energy in July - a crude rebound firms the September 10 move that already carries roughly 70% pricing, on top of core HICP at 2.5% and a composite PMI revised up to 52.0. That makes the cleanest trades the ones with no dollar leg at all: EUR/NZD at a four-point gap, AUD/NZD and GBP/NZD at three, and EUR/CHF at three with the SNB pinned at zero to 2027 and Swiss unemployment now rising to 3.0%. New Zealand remains the short leg at -2 - a cycle ended after one hike by a 5.6% unemployment print, now facing an oil-driven inflation impulse it has no capacity to answer. In the commodity block, USOIL is upgraded from RANGE to LONG on the return of the risk premium, XAU/USD stays a MEDIUM long on the haven bid, and XAG/USD is cut from HIGH to RANGE because silver is now trading the Fed rather than the war and has fallen two sessions running. GER40 comes off to RANGE at 26,171 with rising crude and a firmer ECB both working against a record-high index. Everything reprices again at 12:30Z.

USD.when: Sept 16 FOMC (back in the price on the oil rebound)
USD.note: Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 for a fifth straight meeting with THREE dissents FOR a hike, and Chair Warsh declined to give guidance or submit a dot. That case looked dead 24 hours ago; it is alive again. Governor Lisa Cook told an Anchorage audience that inflation is too high, that she rates the inflation risk above the employment risk, and that she is prepared to act by raising rates. Warsh has said he is open to September if inflation reaccelerates - and WTI back at $77.72 is exactly that reacceleration channel. The labour offset has also thinned: initial claims 199k with a four-week average of 198,750, the lowest of the cycle, announced layoffs the lowest in two years, productivity +1.4% and unit labour costs +1.3%, roughly half expected. The soft reads still on the board are ADP +44k, ISM services employment at 47.4 and JOLTS at 7.14m. June CPI 3.5%, core 2.6%, Q2 GDP 1.5%, payrolls +57k, unemployment 4.2%. July jobs today and July CPI on Aug 12 decide it.

EUR.when: Sept 10 (~70% priced, and the oil rebound helps it)
EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike, ECB headline refi rate 2.40% and marginal lending 2.65%, all confirmed unchanged on Jul 23. The ECB's own July communication is the key text here: it warned the full inflationary impact of the energy shock has yet to emerge, and Lagarde said the longer energy prices stay elevated the more likely they are to drive broader inflation through second-round effects. A crude rebound to $77.72 therefore firms the September case rather than dissolving it. The domestic leg is independently solid - July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5%, services inflation 3.3%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, final composite PMI revised up to 52.0 with services 51.7 and manufacturing 51.9, wage growth 3.4%, unemployment 6.3%. The counterargument remains pipeline disinflation, with producer prices decelerating to 4.6% y/y from 5.9%, and retail sales unexpectedly declining.

GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus. June CPI 2.6%, core 2.6%, services 3.6%. The labour market is firmer than the pause implies - employment +148k in May, wages 4.3%, unemployment 4.9% - and July services PMI jumped to 51.8 from 48.8 with the composite at 52.1. The soft spots are the claimant count rising 6.7k and manufacturing revised down to 51.9. The oil rebound matters for sterling too: the UK is a net energy importer with the most inflation-sensitive committee in the G10 right now, so a sustained crude move firms the hawkish tail rather than the dovish one. TE's end-of-quarter forecast is 4.00%. Q2 GDP on Aug 13 is the first domestic input in two weeks.

JPY.note: Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%. The wage leg is intact - June labour cash earnings rose 3.4% y/y in line with consensus, contractual earnings also 3.4% with full-timers at 3.6%, base pay accelerated to 3.4% from 3.0%, real wages rose 1.6% for a sixth consecutive month, and nominal growth has exceeded 3% for five straight months, the longest run in 34 years. The Bank has also warned for the first time that underlying inflation could exceed its target and said future discussions would focus on upside price risks. What has changed is the market, not the fundamentals: the yen has retraced its intervention gains with USD/JPY back at 158.40 against a 155.20 spike, the 10-year JGB is at 2.79% and climbing with crude, and the Nikkei fell 0.90%. Higher oil is the worst single input for the G10's largest energy importer, and it hits the trade account before it helps the inflation case. Tokyo July core CPI 1.9% from 1.6%; the July Outlook Report's cut to FY2026 CPI of 2.5% is the offset.

AUD.note: Cash rate 4.35% after three hikes in 2026 (Feb, Mar, May) on the energy shock, still the highest in the G10. Q2 trimmed mean 3.6% but the WEIGHTED MEDIAN ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0% from 3.7%, which is not a pause profile - and the crude rebound removes the disinflationary Q3 CPI assumption that underpinned the dovish case. June trade swung to a AUD 1,929m surplus from a 2,367m deficit, though terms of trade slipped to 112 from 117. July services PMI revised up to 53.6 and composite 53.2, unemployment 4.4% with employment +76.3k. Consumer inflation expectations dropped to 4.7% from 5.5% before oil turned. TE's model still carries 4.60%; the market expects no change on Tuesday but the statement is where the risk sits.

NZD.note: OCR raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years, and that cycle is finished. Q2 unemployment printed 5.6% against 5.4% expected, the highest since Q3 2015; underutilisation widened to 13.8%; and the labour cost index slowed to 2.1% y/y. Employment rose 0.5% q/q only because participation climbed to 70.7% from 70.4%. The Q2 CPI of 4.1% that triggered July's move was 27.5% petrol - and with crude turning back up, New Zealand now faces a renewed imported inflation impulse it has no room to answer, which is a worse combination than either problem alone. The offset is domestic sentiment: July business confidence jumped to 56.1 from 36.6, ANZ consumer confidence to 99.3 and the manufacturing PMI to 59.7. Two-year inflation expectations 2.53%; the RBNZ survey lands Aug 13.

CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting. June CPI cooled to 2.8% with CPI-trim and CPI-median BOTH BELOW target as gasoline decelerated sharply. CORRECTION to yesterday's file: June employment was +18,000 with the unemployment rate falling one tenth to 6.5% and average hourly wages up 3.3% y/y - not the +87.8k and 6.6% previously carried. Q1 GDP 0.0% q/q. There is still no rates leg at all, so the loonie remains a pure terms-of-trade trade - but that trade has just turned in its favour, with WTI recovering to $77.72 and Brent to $83.28 as the Hormuz arrangement unravelled. The July jobs report lands today at the same minute as the US print.

CHF.note: At ZERO since mid-2025, held Dec, Mar and Jun; panellists see no change until 2027. July CPI came in at 0.4% y/y against 0.5% expected, down from 0.5%, with core unchanged at 0.3% - under the SNB's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast, and Nomura now models Q3 at 0.5%. July unemployment printed this morning at 3.0%, up from 2.9%, which adds a growth argument on top of the inflation undershoot. Producer and import prices are deflating at -2.1% y/y and FX reserves rose to CHF 758.8bn in June. The June statement pledged to lean against rapid APPRECIATION only; the SNB is content to let the franc slide. The one caveat today is that Hormuz re-escalation bids the haven complex regardless of the policy gap.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz — Iranian parliament reviewing a restrictive transit bill
catalysts.note: The regime has flipped from de-escalation to escalation. Iran struck what it described as hostile targets in the strait after explosions were reported near Qeshm Island. The draft agreement with Oman now under review by the Iranian parliament is materially harsher than markets had priced: US and Israeli vessels barred from transit, countries Tehran deems hostile required to pay compensation before passage, penalties equal to 20% of a vessel's cargo value for violations, and no full reopening until the US lifts its maritime blockade. Iranian officials stated explicitly that the Oman corridor does not fully reopen the waterway. Yesterday's file carried a 60-day interim deal with no transit fees - that was wrong and is corrected. Houthi forces separately claimed attacks on Saudi troop positions and a Saudi oil tanker. WTI $77.72, Brent $83.28. This now feeds the US and euro-area inflation paths directly and is the second-largest input into the September FOMC after today's payrolls.

catalysts.event: Joint US-Japan FX intervention — yen has retraced the entire move
catalysts.note: Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama confirmed the MoF purchased yen in coordination with the US Treasury, the first joint operation since 2011, executed under the September 2025 Joint Statement and aimed at excessive volatility and disorderly movements, with both sides pledging not to hesitate to intervene again. USD/JPY spiked to 155.20 and has since retraced all of it to 158.40, which is precisely the condition that triggered the first operation. The monetary backdrop supports a second - June labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y, base pay accelerating to 3.4%, real wages positive for a sixth month, and the BoJ warning for the first time that underlying inflation could exceed target. Size yen shorts for the possibility of another operation arriving without warning.

The single print that settles the dollar's direction and the September FOMC with it. Consensus around +91k after June's +57k, unemployment expected 4.3% from 4.2%, with April and May already revised down 74k combined. The evidence is now split rather than one-sided: ADP printed +44k against +70k expected and the ISM services employment index fell to 47.4, but initial claims came in at 199k with a four-week average of 198,750 that is the lowest of this cycle, announced layoffs were the lowest in two years and unit labour costs rose just 1.3%, around half expected. A second consecutive sub-100k print with unemployment at 4.3% takes the September hike back out; anything near or above consensus confirms it alongside the oil-driven inflation path.

Lands at the same minute as US payrolls, which is why it is better traded through the crosses than USD/CAD. June was +18,000 with the unemployment rate down a tenth to 6.5% and average hourly wages up 3.3% y/y - a correction to the +87.8k previously carried in this file. With both BoC core measures under target and no rates leg, another soft print leaves the loonie entirely dependent on WTI holding $77.

All four major Australian banks expect a hold at 4.35%, but the internals argue otherwise: the Q2 weighted median ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5%, services inflation to 4.0%, July services PMI was revised up to 53.6 with the composite at 53.2, and June trade swung to a AUD 1,929m surplus. The crude rebound is the new variable - it removes the disinflationary Q3 CPI assumption the dovish case rested on. Against that, consumer inflation expectations collapsed to 4.7% from 5.5% and terms of trade fell to 112 from 117. The key event for AUD/NZD and AUD/CHF.

TE forecasts 3.4% headline after June's 3.5%, with core last at 2.6%. Energy drove more than 60% of a recent monthly gain, so the crude round-trip - down 13% then back up 4% - lands directly in this print and the one after. Note the tension the Fed now faces: ISM services prices paid stayed at 70.3 while the employment index collapsed to 47.4, and unit labour costs came in at 1.3%. Sticky headline inflation with stalled hiring and falling labour costs is the hardest combination for the September committee to resolve.

Sterling's first domestic input in two weeks and the test of whether the hawkish 6-3 hold has an economy behind it. Q1 was +0.6% q/q, July services PMI recovered to 51.8 from 48.8 and the composite to 52.1, but manufacturing was revised down to 51.9 and the claimant count rose 6.7k. A firm print supports a fourth dissenter in September.

Last at 2.53%. With crude turning back up and Q2 CPI at 4.1% having been 27.5% petrol, a rise here would give the Bank cover to retain a tightening bias on Sept 2 even after the 5.6% unemployment print - the main risk to the kiwi short.

The pipeline read on whether the energy round-trip is feeding through to producer costs, and the natural companion to the previous day's CPI. Unit labour costs at 1.3% argue the domestic cost side is benign; the oil side is the variable.

catalysts.event: US retail sales and UoM consumer sentiment
catalysts.note: The demand check. ISM manufacturing at 55.6 and services business activity at 59.1 say demand is fine and it is hiring that has stalled - retail sales is the cleanest test of that split, and the UoM inflation expectations component matters more than usual with energy moving.

Warsh's first Jackson Hole as Chair, and now a very different speech from the one he would have written 48 hours ago. With crude back at $78, Cook publicly prepared to hike and the September meeting live again, the venue becomes the place to signal rather than to explain a pause. Runs Aug 27-28.

The hike is off after Q2 unemployment printed 5.6%, the highest since Q3 2015, with underutilisation at 13.8% and the labour cost index at 2.1%. The OCR stays at 2.50% and the interest is entirely in the language - which is less one-sided than it looks, because July business confidence jumped to 56.1 from 36.6, the manufacturing PMI hit 59.7, and petrol is now reflating rather than unwinding.

A seventh consecutive hold at 2.25% is the base case with both core measures under target and Q1 GDP at 0.0%. The crude rebound removes the disinflationary argument that was building for a cut, which is mildly loonie-supportive - but with June employment at only +18k there is still no policy leg to trade.

Roughly 70% of a hike is priced and the oil rebound reinforces it. The July statement warned the full inflationary impact of the energy shock has yet to emerge and Lagarde said the longer energy prices stay elevated the more likely they are to drive broader inflation through second-round effects - a crude recovery is that scenario. The domestic leg stands alone anyway with July HICP at 2.9%, core 2.5%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and the composite PMI revised up to 52.0. The counterargument is pipeline: producer prices decelerated to 4.6% from 5.9% and retail sales unexpectedly declined.

Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 with three dissents FOR a hike and no guidance or dot from Warsh. The hike is back in the price after Cook said in Anchorage that inflation is too high, that she rates inflation risk above employment risk and that she is prepared to act, with Warsh open to September on reacceleration and crude back at $77.72 supplying it. The soft counter is ADP +44k, ISM services employment 47.4 and JOLTS 7.14m; the hard counter to that is 199k claims, cycle-low layoffs and unit labour costs at 1.3%. Today's payrolls and the Aug 12 CPI decide it.

TE forecasts a hold at 3.75%, but the Jul 30 vote was 6-3 against a 7-2 consensus and July services PMI swung back into expansion at 51.8 with the composite at 52.1. An energy shock in a net-importing economy hardens the hawkish tail; a fourth dissenter would confirm it. The counterarguments are the downwardly revised manufacturing PMI at 51.9 and a claimant count rising 6.7k.

A hold at 1.00% remains the base case with October the live window. The Bank has now warned for the first time that underlying inflation could exceed its target and said future policy discussions would focus on upside price risks. June labour cash earnings rose 3.4% in line with consensus, base pay accelerated to 3.4% from 3.0%, real wages rose 1.6% for a sixth straight month and nominal growth has exceeded 3% for five months, the longest run in 34 years. Takata is dissenting for 1.25% and Tamura wants a neutral rate near 2%. The new complication is crude at $78, which hits Japan's trade account before it helps the inflation case.

A hold at 0% is universally expected, with panellists seeing no change until 2027, July CPI at 0.4% undershooting the Bank's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast and unemployment now rising to 3.0%. The relevance is language: the June statement pledged to lean against rapid franc APPRECIATION only, and any hardening of that is the main cap on EUR/CHF, GBP/CHF and AUD/CHF.

geopolitics: The Hormuz situation has reversed direction and the correction matters more than the level. Yesterday's read described a 60-day interim arrangement with inbound traffic through an Iranian-controlled route, outbound through Omani waters and no transit fees or tolls, awaiting only a final sign-off. The terms that have since emerged are considerably harsher. The draft now under review by the Iranian parliament would bar US and Israeli vessels from transiting the strait altogether, require countries Tehran deems hostile to pay compensation before being granted passage, impose penalties equal to 20% of a vessel's cargo value on violators, and make any full reopening conditional on the United States first lifting its maritime blockade. Iranian officials have said publicly that the arrangement with Oman does not fully reopen the waterway and that Iran will not return it to the status of an open international strait, insisting on a measure of permanent control - which is the sovereignty question the whole negotiation has always turned on. On the ground the conflict is escalating rather than settling: Iran struck what it described as hostile targets in the strait after explosions were reported near Qeshm Island, the UK Navy reported explosions near a tanker in transit, and Houthi forces in Yemen claimed attacks on Saudi troop positions and on a Saudi oil tanker while threatening further vessels in the Red Sea. The market response has been immediate. WTI has recovered to $77.72 from $74.79, a two-session gain of roughly 4% that leaves it up 5.71% on the month and 21.67% on the year, with Brent at $83.28. The transmission into FX has therefore reversed too, and in a way that is the mirror image of yesterday: a rebuilding energy premium raises the US inflation path, which raises the Fed path, which raises real rates - and that is why silver has fallen for two straight sessions to $62.03 while gold has held $4,250.77 on the haven bid. The two metals have decoupled, and the split is the cleanest available read on which force is dominant for any given asset. The euro is the principal beneficiary among the currencies, because the ECB explicitly tied its July bias to the energy channel; CAD recovers its terms-of-trade leg; NZD is the principal casualty, with a Q2 CPI that was 27.5% petrol and a central bank that has stopped; and JPY, as the G10's largest energy importer, takes the trade-account hit that offsets its otherwise improving wage story. The genuine two-sided risk is the Iranian parliamentary process itself - the bill has not passed, the US concession it demands has not been made, and either development would unwind the last two sessions as quickly as they were built. That is why USOIL is a MEDIUM long rather than a high-conviction one.
